title: Anesthesia in patients with Brugada syndrome: two case reports
case_prompt: A 31-year-old Filipino laborer was scheduled for a laparoscopic appendectomy. He had no significant medical history. Preoperative vital signs were stable, with a temperature of 37.9°C. General anesthesia was induced with fentanyl, propofol, and rocuronium, and maintained with sevoflurane along with intermittent doses of fentanyl and rocuronium. The operation lasted 2 hours with minimal blood loss and stable vital signs. During emergence, after administration of atropine and neostigmine, the patient developed sudden ventricular tachycardia with undetectable blood pressure and pulse. Cardiopulmonary resuscitation was initiated, including two 1 mg doses of intravenous epinephrine and one defibrillation, restoring normal sinus rhythm and baseline vital signs. An arterial blood gas analysis showed no severe metabolic acidosis. He was transferred to the intensive care unit for observation. Further testing—including 12-lead ECG, CK-MB, troponin-T, echocardiography, and C-reactive protein—was unremarkable except for a 12-lead ECG in the recovery room that showed coved-type ST-segment elevations in leads V2 and V3 and, later that day, a saddleback pattern in lead V2.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Myocardial ischemia or infarction was considered but excluded because postoperative cardiac enzymes and serial ECG were normal — “The normal postoperative cardiac enzyme and serial ECG studies rule out the possibility of myocardial ischemia.”
2. Long QT syndrome was considered as part of the differential for intraoperative ventricular arrhythmias — “Long QT syndrome (LQTS) with polymorphic VT.”
3. Catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricular tachycardia was included in the differential — “Catecholaminergic polymorphic VT.”
4. Short QT syndrome was included in the differential of intraoperative ventricular arrhythmias — “Short QT syndrome.”
5. Hyperkalemia was considered because electrolyte disturbances can unmask arrhythmias but excluded as the patient had no preoperative electrolyte imbalance — “a young man had no any systemic disease history, preoperation electrolyte imbalance, or hypothermia, and normal ECG.”
6. Hypercalcemia was considered but excluded on the same basis — “a young man had no any systemic disease history, preoperation electrolyte imbalance, or hypothermia, and normal ECG.”
7. Hypothermia was considered but excluded as the patient had no hypothermia — “a young man had no any systemic disease history, preoperation electrolyte imbalance, or hypothermia, and normal ECG.”
8. Brugada syndrome was considered when follow-up ECG demonstrated characteristic ST-segment elevations and later confirmed by genetics — “Brugada syndrome with the characteristic ECG changes was the most probable cause, and later the genetic study confirmed the diagnosis.”
